newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Strike shuts Coca-Cola plants in Sri Lanka.
newsitem.headline: Strike shuts Coca-Cola plants in Sri Lanka.

text.p: A strike by union labour protesting against planned layoffs has shut down Coca-Cola Co production in Sri Lanka, company and union officials said on Friday.

More than 700 workers are on strike at two bottling plants run by Pure Beverages Co Ltd, the island's sole local Coke bottler, a 51 percent subsidiary of F&NCC, Coke's regional bottler based in Singapore.
F&NCC, a joint venture of Coca-Cola and Singapore's Fraser & Neave, bought the controlling stake in Pure Beverages for $13 million in November 1994.
The Sri Lankan firm earlier operated as a Coke franchise.
The labour dispute began when F&NCC offered a voluntary retirement scheme to get rid of what it said was excess labour.
The company then shut down its plant at Kaduwela, offering workers temporary employment at the second plant at Biyagama. Union workers at both plants went on strike on December 12.
Both Kaduwela and Biyagama are north of the capital, Colombo.
"The company decided to close its Kaduwela plant because the Biyagama plant can meet the island's entire demand," a Pure Beverages spokesman told Reuters.
The company had made significant financial losses in the past two years and it was not economically viable to operate two plants, he said.
Workers were offered a 40-month voluntary retirement scheme from June 1996 and the Labour Commissioner is reviewing the company's application to lay off 350 workers.
Analysts said the strike had had no visible impact on the market as there were plenty of other soft drinks available.

Bala Tampoe, leader of the Ceylon Mercantile Union, which represents the workers, said the union was demanding that the company reopen the Kaduwela plant as a condition for ending the strike at Biyagama.
"For us jobs are vital," he told Reuters. "That's why we refuse the offer. You can't have an involuntary voluntary retirement scheme."

Avanka Herath, food and beverage industry analyst at brokerage Jardine Fleming HNB, said the company wanted to shut down one plant to improve its bottom line. "We forecast a loss of 88.1 million rupees ($1.5 million) for the financial year ending March 1997," he told Reuters.

"If they settle the labour dispute we expect a turnaround and a profit of 25 million rupees (for the year to March 1998) on the assumption that they will shut the Kaduwela plant and start production at Biyagama by March this year," he said.
The company made a loss of 19.5 million rupees ($342,000) in 1996.
